Since you'll be directing the phases, here's my suggested roadmap for how this typically breaks down (as a reference — you decide what we actually do and when): ## Proposed phase roadmap (for discussion) **Phase 1 — Document structure & tokenizer skeleton** - Define the core data types: `Document`, `Node`, `Token` - Read raw HTML from a file/stdin into memory - Basic tokenizer: split input into text vs. tags by scanning for `<` and `>` **Phase 2 — Tag parsing** - Parse tag names, distinguish start tags (`
`), end tags (`
`), and self-closing tags (`
`) - Handle attributes: `name="value"`, single-quoted, unquoted, boolean attributes **Phase 3 — DOM tree building** - Build the tree: push nodes on a stack as start tags arrive, pop on end tags - Handle mismatched/unclosed tags gracefully - Pretty-print the tree for debugging **Phase 4 — Robustness** - Comments ``, DOCTYPE, CDATA - Whitespace and text-node handling rules - Special-cases: `

# Context: Understanding a Mini HTML Parser I am sharing the concept of an assignment so you can understand what the project is about. This is for your understanding only, not a request to implement anything. ## 1. Project Concept The assignment is to understand how a basic HTML parser works internally. The idea is to take an HTML file, understand its structure, represent that structure as a DOM (Document Object Model) tree in memory, and display the tree in a format similar to the Linux `tree` command. The same concept will eventually be explored independently in C and Python. ## 2. Example HTML Input Consider a file named `page.html` containing: ```html

Hello

Welcome to AI Karyashala

Learn by doing

``` ## 3. Example Expected Output The HTML structure is represented as a tree: ```text . └── html └── body ├── h1 │ └── "Hello" ├── p [class="intro", id="first"] │ └── "Welcome to AI Karyashala" └── p [class="note"] └── "Learn by doing" ``` Here: - `.` represents the document root. - `html` is an element containing `body`. - `body` contains three child elements: `h1` and two `p` elements. - Each element can contain other elements or text nodes. - Attributes such as `class` and `id` belong to their respective elements. - The tree shows structural relationships, not the original HTML indentation. ## 4. Core Concepts **HTML parsing:** Reading HTML and identifying its elements, attributes, closing tags, and text. **DOM tree:** A tree data structure representing the hierarchical structure of the document. **Element node:** Represents an HTML element and holds its tag name, attributes, and child nodes. **Text node:** Represents the text contained between HTML tags. **Parent and child relationships:** For example, `body` is the parent of `h1`, and `h1` is the parent of the text node `"Hello"`. **Tree traversal:** Visiting nodes in the DOM tree to display the correct hierarchy and order. The important distinction is that the program must represent the HTML as an actual tree in memory. Simply examining the original HTML lines and printing similar-looking output is not the same as constructing and traversing a DOM. ## 5. Scope and Constraints The assignment focuses on a small subset of HTML. Supported concepts include: - Opening and closing tags. - Text content. - Nested and sibling elements. - Attributes with double-quoted values. - Ignoring whitespace that exists only for indentation. The assignment does not require a complete browser or full HTML5 parser. JavaScript, CSS, HTML entities, and browser rendering are outside the required scope. Existing HTML parsing libraries, such as Python's `html.parser`, BeautifulSoup, `lxml`, and `libxml2`, must not be used. The parser must also detect unexpected closing tags, mismatched closing tags, and unclosed elements. ## 6. Command-Line Examples The intended program will eventually support commands such as: ```bash domparser page.html domparser page.html --tree domparser page.html --text domparser page.html --find-tag p domparser page.html --find-id first domparser page.html --find-class intro ``` These commands represent different ways to display or search the same DOM structure. ## 7. Tools and Development Context The assignment involves three development tools: - **OpenCode:** An AI coding assistant. - **Entire:** A tool used to capture development context and connect it with commits. - **GitHub:** A platform for storing the source code and its development history. The C and Python implementations must be developed independently, and both should produce the same output for equivalent input files. The main educational goal is to understand the concepts and decisions involved in software development, rather than merely obtaining working code. ## Your role Treat everything above as project context. Understand the terminology, example, expected behavior, and restrictions so this information can guide our future conversations. Do not implement the project, generate code, create or modify files, execute commands, or propose an implementation plan. For now, this is only a conceptual explanation of the assignment.

## What I Understand

**Goal:** A mini HTML parser (`domparser`) that:
1. Reads a subset of HTML from a file
2. Builds a **real DOM tree in memory** (element nodes + text nodes, with parent/child relationships)
3. Traverses that tree to produce `tree`-style output, extract text, or search (`--tree`, `--text`, `--find-tag`, `--find-id`, `--find-class`)

**Supported subset:**
- Opening/closing tags, nested & sibling elements
- Attributes with double-quoted values (e.g., `class="intro"`)
- Text content as child nodes (shown as `"Hello"`)
- Indentation-only whitespace ignored

**Explicitly out of scope:**
- No parsing libraries (`libxml2`, `html.parser`, BeautifulSoup, lxml) — hand-rolled parsing only
- No JS, CSS, entities, rendering, or full HTML5 spec handling

**Must handle errors:** unexpected closing tags, mismatched closing tags, unclosed elements.

**Key design constraint:** The output must come from *traversing the actual tree structure*, not from echoing formatted input lines — the DOM is the source of truth.

**Process notes:**
- C and Python versions are separate implementations but must produce identical output for equivalent inputs
- Development happens with OpenCode + Entire + GitHub
- The educational journey (decisions, reasoning) matters as much as the code

## Points I'll keep in mind when we build

- Tree structure in C: nodes with tag name, attribute list, children, and a text-node type — memory management (allocation/free) will be a first-class concern
- Parser needs a stack-based approach to match open/close tags and detect the three error cases
- Output formatting (`├──`, `└──`, `│`) requires tracking depth and "is-last-child" state during traversal

Answer the question: yes, clang domparser.c works, produces a.out.

Yes, absolutely! That's the simplest way to compile:

```bash
clang domparser.c
```

**What happens:** Clang compiles the code and, since you didn't specify an output name, creates an executable with the default name **`a.out`**. You then run it like this:

```bash
./a.out page.html
```

## So why did I suggest `-o domparser`?

The `-o` flag just lets you **name the output file** yourself:

| Command | Executable produced | Run it with |
|---|---|---|
| `clang domparser.c` | `a.out` | `./a.out page.html` |
| `clang -o domparser domparser.c` | `domparser` | `./domparser page.html` |

Both work identically — it's purely about naming. `a.out` is a historical default ("assembler output") and naming it `domparser` matches the assignment's intended command name (`domparser page.html`), so it reads a bit nicer.

## What about `-Wall -Wextra`?

Those are optional too — they don't change how the program runs, they just make clang **warn you about suspicious code** (unused variables, missing returns, etc.). Since this is a learning project, I'd recommend keeping them; they teach you good habits. But they're not required to compile.

**Three valid choices, pick your style:**

```bash
clang domparser.c                                   # simplest → a.out
clang -o domparser domparser.c                      # named output
clang -Wall -Wextra -o domparser domparser.c        # named + warnings (my recommendation)
```

Phase 1 is complete and verified. Here's what was implemented:

## Files created

**`page.html`** — the sample HTML input file from the assignment.

**`domparser.c`** — the Phase 1 C program:

| Component of the code | What it does |
|---|---|
| `if (argc < 2)` | Checks the user provided a file path; prints usage and exits with failure if not |
| `fopen(argv[1], "r")` | Opens the HTML file for reading |
| `perror("Error opening file")` | Reports the exact OS-level reason (e.g., "No such file or directory") if open fails |
| `static char buffer[MAX_SIZE]` | 1 MB buffer in BSS (initialized data segment, not the stack) to hold the file |
| `fread(buffer, 1, MAX_SIZE - 1, fp)` | Reads up to 1 MB − 1 bytes of the file into memory in one shot |
| `fclose(fp)` | Closes the file immediately after reading |
| `buffer[n] = '\0'` | Null-terminates the bytes so it's a valid C string |
| `if (n == 0)` | Detects an empty file and reports it |
| `printf("%s", buffer)` + trailing-newline check | Prints the file, adding a `\n` only if the file didn't end with one |
| `EXIT_SUCCESS / EXIT_FAILURE` | Standard exit codes (0 and 1) |

## Verified behavior

- ✅ Compiles clean with `clang -Wall -Wextra` (zero warnings)
- ✅ `./domparser page.html` prints the full file with indentation preserved
- ✅ `./domparser` (no args) → usage message, exit code 1
- ✅ `./domparser nope.html` → "Error opening file: No such file or directory", exit code 1

Phase 1 proves end-to-end file I/O: **argument → open → read → print**. Ready for Phase 2 whenever you want to guide the next step (likely: tokenizing into tags/text).

Running the Phase 1 code is a two-step process: **compile** (turn the C source into an executable), then **run** (execute it with an HTML file). ## Step 1: Compile In the terminal, from the project folder (`/home/pavanlanka/task47`): ```bash clang -o domparser domparser.c ``` This creates an executable file named `domparser` in the same folder. You only need to re-run this step **when you change the `.c` file**. *(The simplest form `clang domparser.c` also works — it just names the output `a.out` instead.)* ## Step 2: Run ```bash ./domparser page.html ``` - `./` tells the shell to run the program from the **current directory** (it's not in your system's PATH) - `page.html` is the argument the program will open, read, and print ## What you'll see The contents of `page.html` printed to your terminal: ```html

Hello

Welcome to AI Karyashala

Learn by doing

``` ## Trying the error cases ```bash ./domparser # missing argument → Usage: ./domparser ./domparser fake.html # bad filename → Error opening file: No such file or directory ``` ## Handy shortcut Chain compile + run so you never forget to recompile after editing: ```bash clang -o domparser domparser.c && ./domparser page.html ``` The `&&` means: only run if compilation succeeded (this is exactly the command I used to verify Phase 1). The program already exists and is compiled in your project folder — you can run `./domparser page.html` right now to see it work.
